145th Psi Upsilon
Convention
W ot since 1929 have the undergradu
ates and alumni of Psi Upsilon Fraternity
traveled to this nation's capital for a con
vention. Washington, D.C. A city of
magnificent monuments and fascinating
museums. A city of imposing federal of
fice buildings and impressive foreign em
bassies. A city pulsing with the heartbeat
of the United States of America. Let us
hope that the vitality and energy that are
the trademarks of our surroundings will
infect us all �
that they will inspire each
of us in all that we say and do at this
145th Convention.
Much has changed in the fifty-nine year
period since the Eta Chapter hosted the
96th Convention in Washington, D.C.
This year's host, for instance, the Phi Beta
Chapter at the College of William and
Mary, was not to be founded until fiftyfive years aft:er that auspicious event. The
thirty-eighth chapter of Psi Upsilon was
chartered on April 14, 1984, in Williams
burg, Virginia. It represents the newest
and one of the brightest jewels in our
illustrious crovin.
The 1929 Convention counted among
its participants five United States Sena
tors, one member of the House of Rep
resentatives, the Secretary of State
(Henry L. Stimson, Beta '88), and the
Chief Justice ofthe Supreme Court, who
formerly had been President ofthe United
States (William H. Taft, Beta '78). It in
cluded a reception by President Hoover
on the White House lawn, visits to the
House and Senate where delegates were
received by Vice President Curtis, and a
formal gathering in the diplomatic re
ception room of the State Department.
The Psi Upsilon Fratemity of today
cannot match those unbelievably im
pressive facts. But we can count among
our brothers some of Washington, D.C.'s
outstanding leaders: William H. Webs
ter, Gamma '45, Director of the Central
Intelligence Agency; John Paul Stevens,
Omega '41, Supreme Court Justice; Wil
liam S. Cohen, Kappa '62, United States
Senator; and Samuel S. Stratton, Upsilon
'37, United States Congressman, to name
just a few.
Yes, much has changed since 1929. Yet
so much has remained the same. An ex
cerpt from the annual communication of
that year reads:
"The college fraternity would seem to
be an established institution in the col
leges and universities of North America,
particularly as several of these fratemi
ties are older than half of the colleges and
universities themselves; but age alone is
not justification for the continuance of
any institution."
Much has changed in the
fifty-nine year period since
the Eta Chapter hosted the
96th Convention in
Washington, D.C.
No, age alone was not adequate jus
tification for the continuance of an insti
tution (in this case our beloved fraternity)
in 1929, nor is it today. But we are being
challenged today to justify that existence
hke we have never been challenged be
fore. The image of college fraternities has
been suUied by such incidents as the tragic
death of a freshman pledge at Rutgers
University, alleged gang rapes at the
University of Rochester and Florida State
University, vulgar and tasteless rush
functions at the University of Pennsyl
vania, alleged racism at the University of:
Wisconsin, outrageous hazing practices
at the University of Texas, to name just
a few. None of these incidents involved
Psi Upsilon, but each affected the way
we are perceived by the general public.
These and hundreds of other negative
incidents involving fratemities have re-i
ceived extensive press coverage and have
precipitated public outcries.
Some educators believe that
fraternities are anachronistic,
that they hamper academic
performance, . . .
Some educators befieve that fi-aterni
ties are anachronistic, that they hamper
academic performance, that they pro-s
mote non-intellectual or anti-intellectual
attitudes, that they impede the social and
moral maturation of students, that they
foster an adversarial attitude in their:
members toward the college or univer
sity, that they promote sexism, that they
engender arrogance and hypocrisy, that
they are downright dangerous. What is
our response?
Psi Upsilon was founded to promote:
"the highest moral, intellectual and social
excellence and educational standards in
all its members." Those tenets are just
as relevant in 1988 as they were in 1833.

uting to or impeding the social and morali

Fraternity News From Across the Continent
I PLEDGE ALLEGIANCE . . .
(Indianapolis, IN) Pledges are not only
an issue in national elections! A different
type of pledge (as in the orientation pe
riod a
prospective member goes through
in fraternities before being initiated) is
now the subject of hot debate among the
leaders of the 57 college fraternities. It
has always been said that if there were
no pledges, there would be no hazing.
So, argues the Fraternity Executives As
sociation, a professional organization of
the chief executive officers of college fra
ternities, why not just abohsh pledging?!
Whether this new idea will sweep North
America, and whether this will necessi
tate the reorganization of our entire fra
temity, remains to be seen. But one fra
ternity, Zeta Beta Tau, has finished
debating the issue and has actually abol
ished pledging periods in its chapters.
Sure to be a subject of intense debate,
the 146th Convention, to be held August
17-20 in Chicago, will consider this issue.
Allison Roseman, Gamma '89 (left),
and Amy Weber, Gamma '89, accept the
1988 Psi Upsilon Award for Academic
Distinction for their chapter from Bill
Robie, President ofthe Executive Coun
cil, at the 145th Convention in August.
HOOT, HOOT HOORAY!
(Amherst, MA) The Gamma Chapter at
Amherst College received the 1988 Psi
Upsilon Award for Academic Distinction.
Amy Weber '89 and AlUson Roseman '89
accepted the award for the Chapter at
the awards branch ofthe 145th Conven
tion in Washington, D.C. in August. In
deciding to award the Gamma with this
honor, the Convention cited the Chap
ter's outstanding scholarship program
which is designed to assist members with
their studies, and the eight seniors who
received honors at graduation (one summa
cum laiide, four magna cum laude, and
three cum laude). Not bad for a school
that "discontinued" its fraternity system
in 1984!
NOT A CRISIS: A CHALLENGE
(Boston, MA) The liability insurance cri
sis in the United States has attracted much
attention and dramatically affected our
lives. Insurance rates have skyrocketed
(with the ripple effects forcing rates up
in Canada, as well), long-standing prac
tices and traditions have been altered or
eliminated for safety's sake, and some
businesses have been forced into bank
ruptcy.: Fraternities were not spared this
turmoil. Most of our chapters were underinsured. Several chapters were una
ble to purchase insurance at any price.
The Kappa Chapter was ordered by Bow
doin College to close its doors unless it
could find sufficient insurance �
insur
ance that no
company was wiUing to is
sue. Our angel of mercy was James A.
Swanke, Jr., Rho '80. Brother Swanke is
a nationally recognized expert in the risk
management field. Under his guidance,
the International Office conducted a
thorough review of our
chapters' current
and future insurance needs, including an
inspection of each chapter house. With
this information, Psi Upsilon elected to
join the Fratemity Insurance Purchasing
Group, Inc. , an
organization of college
fraternities through which a master liabihty insurance policy was purchased at
a reduced premium. Our chapters and
alumni associations now have far greater
protection at a lower price than ever be
fore. Psi Upsilon no longer risks insol
vency at the mere threat of a lawsuit. For
that we are forever indebted to Jim
Swanke. But better insurance coverage
does not diminish the responsibihty all
of us have to ensure safe and responsible
behavior in our chapters.
THOU SHALT BE FRUITFUL
(Atlanta, GA) Ask the average member
of a smaller chapter what they remmeber
most about chapter meetings and they
would probably respond that someone al
most always got up to say "If everyone
would just recruit one person, we'd dou
ble our membership!" Well, the Gamma
Tau Chapter at the Georgia Institute of
Technology stopped discussing it and ac
tually did it! Since its founding in 1970,
the Gamma Tau has suffered the distinc
tion of being "the new fratemity" in a
system of very old and established Greek
letter societies. Additionally, the Gamma
Tau Chapter house is located a fair dis
tance from the main part of campus and
is, shall we say . . .
inadequate. But this
year the strong membership refused to
take "no" for an answer. Led by Rush
Chairmen Rob Schmidt and Brian Cum
mings and with a strong assist from Field
Director T. J. Turner, the Chapter suc
ceeded in recruiting an
outstanding group
of new members. We heartily offer the
Gamma Tau our congratulations and look
forward to seeing, in person, the results
of thefr outstanding work at the 1990
Convention, to be held August 16-19 in
Atlanta, Georgia!
BRICKS PLUS MORTAR DOES NOT
EQUAL FRATERNITY
(Berkeley, CA) "You can't start a frater
nity at Cal Berkeley without a house."
At least that is what everyone kept telhng
us. The Executive Council was very anx
ious to reactivate the Epsilon Chapter at
the University of Caltfornia, which had
gone inactive in 1972, but was dissuaded
from doing so for more than 10 years by
those who said it couldn't be done with
out a house. Finally, in 1985, the Epsilon
was reactivated without a house, but with
an
incredibly strong and motivated group
of men. Soon afterwards, two miracles
occurred. A house became available close
to campus, incredible in Berkeley's tight
housing market, and a committed group
of alumni led by Bill Brown, Epsilon '63,
offered to buy the house for the Chapter.
The Epsilon flourished in its new home.
Unfortunately, at least for now, this story

3
does not have a happy ending. The City
of Berkeley decided to enforce its ex
tremely restrictive zoning regulations,
declaring that the building could no longer
be used as a fraternity house. Un
daunted, the undergraduates and alumni
obtained office space for meetings and,
despite this enormous setback, the Chap
ter has still managed to operate and rush
effectively. Our oldest chapters existed
quite nicely for 50-odd years without
chapter houses. Times have changed,
though. Maybe, in the long-run, you can't
have a fratemity at Berkeley without a
house. But in the short-run, as the Ep
silon has proven, you sure can put up a
good fight. A hearty "Psi, Psi, Psi" to the
Epsilon undergraduates and alumni!
TU-WHIT, TU-WHERE?
(All over North America!) Psi Upsilon is
not, and should not be, an experience
that ends at graduation. A tremendous
number of our alumni are involved in the
alumni associations of their own chapter
or of a chapter located where they now
reside. Their assistance and advice in
managing our chapters are indispensa
ble. The alumni organizations also pro
vide them with a forum to remain in con
tact with old friends and to make new
ones. But so many of our alumni live in
areas far from their college, in areas lack
ing an active chapter of Psi Upsilon.
Unfortunately, at least at the present
time, Psi Upsilon does not have under
graduate chapters in Washington, D.C,
Buffalo, New York, or the State of Flor
ida, just to name a few. Fortunately that
small problem has not prevented alumni
in those areas from gathering. Elmira,
New York, Washington, D.C, Balti
more, Maryland, Naples, Florida, and
Buffalo, New York are just a few of the
cities in which alumni have formed re
gional alumni associations. In Washing
ton, alumni gather at monthly luncheons
for socializing and a httle networking. In
Elmira, alumni congregate for an annual
dinner that features a rousing chorus of
virtually every Psi U song in the book!
Just because you may be located in an
area far from your own chapter or from
any chapter does not mean you cannot
experience the benefits of becoming an
involved alumnus. If you would like to
find out ff there is a regional alumni as
sociation in your area, or if you are in
terested in starting one, please call the
Intemational Office at (215) 647-4830 for
help, advice, and encouragement!

SPEAKING OF THE FOUNDATION
The First Thirty Years
All the brothers I know, alumni and undergraduates alike, are inter
ested in their own chapter first and foremost. That's just the way it
should be, too.
Happily a remarkable number of Psi U's see beyond this to the "na
tional," realizing that the strength and health of their chapters, perhaps
their very life, are directly related to the strength and health of the
"national.
"
Most of us know relatively little about the "national" �
in fact that
ours is an "international," in recognition of our great Canadian brothers.
Further, fewer still understand that the international consists of two
entities: the Psi Upsilon Fraternity and The Psi Upsilon Foundation,
Inc.
I submit that it may be important to become aware of this duality.
Both are Psi Upsilon. Both are designed to support and advance the
same objectives. Both work hand in hand. The Foundation, however,
only recently has emerged as a key element in the life of Psi Upsilon.
It is coming of age and is destined to play an increasingly significant
role in the future.
This is the first of several articles to describe that role.
It was on May 16, 1958 that The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. ,
an
educational and philanthropic corporation, was duly incorporated in the
State of Rhode Island. Edward T. Richards, Sigma '27, a prominent
Providence attorney, alumni leader of the Brown University Chapter,
and Executive Council member since 1939, was a prime mover.
The stated purposes, as set forth in the Articles of Incorporation,
include the following:
(1) To provide financial assistance to needy and deserving students in
good standing at colleges and universities in the United States and
Canada.
(2) To provide improved or additional educational reference material
or equipment for students at such colleges and universities.
(3) To provide intellectual guidance and encouragement to students
through visitation, counseling, presentation of intellectual material, or
by establishment of forms of recognition of intellectual interest or
achievement.
(4) To supplement the work of such colleges and universities in the
encouragement ofand promotion of scholarship, character, and morality.
Prophetic words were written at the launching of that enterprise more
than thirty years ago, when the announcement of the Foundation's es
tablishment went out to the 17,000 living alumni of that day:
"The Foundation will help to meet the challenge of the future �
the
growing necessity for well educated, dedicated men who will serve their
country, their college, and their Fraternity for generations to come."
You will be hearing more. . . .

CONVENTION '88
Fostering basic fraternal values proves
to he theme of 145th Convention
(Washington, D.C.) The excitement at the hub of the
nation's government in an election year made Washing
ton D.C. an excellent place for Psi Upsilon to meet for
its convention in August 1988. The Hyatt Arlington Hotel
and its General Manager, Richard Carlson, Epsilon Nu
'69, provided an outstanding "home" for the fraternity
throughout the event.
The excitement began on Thursday, August 25, when
the convention was opened by Stephen T. Selby, Phi
Beta '89, undergraduate president ofthe Phi Beta Chap
ter, host of this year's annual event. A thought-provoking
presentation was given that first evening by Will S. Keim,
who currently is pursuing his Ph.D. at Oregon State
University. "Demythologizing the Animal House," a
moving talk on the role of college fraternities in the
1980's, set the tone for three intense days of work and
play. Representatives from 32 of Psi Upsilon's 33 chap
ters topped off" the evening by attending a festive "Wel
come to Virginia" reception hosted by the members of
the Phi Beta Chapter.
Charting the course for the upcoming year is the
mission that each Psi Upsilon convention sets out to
accomplish. This year the delegates took their respon
sibilities to heart and undertook actions that will not only
affect Psi Upsilon for the coming year but well into the
future. Included in the legislation that was adopted by
the 145th convention was: the adoption of a master lia
bility insurance policy and a strict premium payment
enforcement procedure, determination and adoption of
an operating budget for the 1988-89 fiscal year, deter
mination of a
policy strongly discouraging "little sister"
organizations in Psi Upsilon chapters, a review ofthe Psi
Upsilon Constitution, and the adoption of a new policy
for the acceptance of chapters into the fraternity.
The chairmen ofthe various legislative committees had
much work to accomplish during the three day event:
getting their committees organized, seeing that the leg
islation was written, and assuring that the work of the
committee was given careful consideration by the del
egates at large. These key people were: Charles M. Hall,
Nu Alpha '71, Committee on Budget and Development;
Edward G. Mitzen, Pi '89, Committee on New Business;
Murray A. Kahn, Theta Theta '90, Committee on Un
finished Business; John K. Menzies, Pi '41, Committee
on Credentials and Nominations; and Thomas A. Leg
horn, Delta '77, Rules Committee. The general meetings
were ably chaired by William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega
'66, President of the Executive Council.
This year, as well, a Task Force on Critical Issues was
appointed to facilitate an in-depth discussion on some of
the issues facing the college fi-atemity on today's campus.

Force, led a series of discussions on hazing, alcohol use
and abuse, sexism, and the negative view of fraternities
that seems to be apparent in the press and among many

Risk Management Policy
The Risk Management Policy of the Fraternity Insurance Purchasing Group includes the
provisions which follow and shall apply to all fraternity entities and all levels of fraternity
membership.
ALCOHOL AND DRUGS
1. The possession, use and/or consumption of ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES, while on chap
ter premises, during an official fraternity event, or in any situation sponsored or endorsed
by the chapter, must be in comphance with any and all applicable laws of the state,
province, county, city and university.
2. No alcoholic beverages may be purchased through the chapter treasury nor may the
purchase of same for members or guests be undertaken or coordinated by any member
in the name of or on behalf of the chapter.
3. No chapter members, collectively or individually, shall purchase for, serve to, or sell
alcoholic beverages to any minor (i.e., those under legal "drinking age").
4. The possession, sale and/or use of any ILLEGAL DRUGS or CONTROLLED SUB
STANCES at any chapter house, sponsored event or at any event that an observer would
associate with the fraternity, is .strictly prohibited.
5. No chapter may co-sponsor an event with an alcoholic distributor, charitable organization
or tavern (tavern defined as an establishment generating more than half of annual gross
sales from alcohol) where alcohol is given away, sold or otherwise provided to those
present.
6. No chapter may co-sponsor or co-linance a function where alcohol is purchased by any
of the host chapters, groups or organizations.
7. All rush activities associated with any chapter will be a DRY rush function.
8. OPEN PARTIES, meaning those with unrestricted access by non-members ofthe fra
ternity, without specific invitation, shall be prohibited.
9. No member shall permit, tolerate, encourage or participate in "drinking games."
10. No alcohol shall be present at any pledge/associate member/novice program or activity
of the chapter.
HAZING
No chapter shall conduct hazing activities. Hazing activities are defined as;
"Any action taken or situation created, intentionally, whether on or off fraternity jjremises,
to produce mental or physical discomfort, embarrassment, harassment, or riducule. Such
activities may include but are not limited to the following: use of alcohol; paddling in any
form; creation of excessive fatigue; physical and psychological shocks; quests, treasure hunts,
scavenger hunts, road trips or any other such activities carried on outside or inside of the
confines ofthe chapter hoilse; wearing of public apparel which is conspicuous and not normally
in good taste; engaging in public stunts and buffoonery; morally degrading or humiliating
games and activities; and any other activities which are not consistent with fraternal law,
ritual or policy or the regulations and policies ofthe educational institution."
SEXUAL ABUSE
The fraternity will not tolerate or condone any form of sexually abusive behavior on the part
of its members, whether physical, mental or emotional. This is to include any actions which
are demeaning to women including but not hmited to date rape, gang rape or verbal harrassment.
FIRE, HEALTH AND SAFETY
I. All chapter houses shall, prior to, during, and following occupancy, meet all local fire and
health codes and standards.
2. All chapters must have posted by common phones, emergency numbers for fire, police
and ambulance and must have posted evacuation routes from chapter houses, common
areas as well as posted on the back of the door of each sleeping room.
3. All chapters shall comply with engineering recommendations as reported by the insurance
company.
EDUCATION
Each student member, associate member and pledge shall be instructed annually on the Risk
Management Policy of the Fraternity Insurance Purchasing Group.
